505.title: Ahalya restored
505.hook: an empty hermitage on the road to Mithila, and the woman nobody can see
505.howItsDone: Ahalya is honored in Hindu tradition as one of the panchakanya, five women whose names some Hindus recite in a well-known morning verse; her story is told very differently across tellings, and discussions of it often turn on those differences.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the weapons, part three. Maricha hurled over the sea, alive, and a sacrifice completed. Did you leave someone a way to walk off whole? Now the road turns toward Mithila. Day five hundred five.

With the sacrifice done, the hermits at Siddhashrama have a plan. King Janaka of Mithila is holding a great sacrifice, they tell Rama, and he keeps a bow there you should see. So they walk north, for days, and every evening the sage tells stories: how the Ganga came down from heaven, how the ocean was churned. Then, just outside Mithila, they pass an old hermitage. Lovely, but completely empty. No smoke from the fire, no voices. Rama asks: whose was this, and why is no one here?
screen: `NORTH, TOWARD MITHILA.` → `STORIES EVERY EVENING.` → `AN EMPTY HERMITAGE.`

segments.voice: Vishvamitra tells him. This was the hermitage of the great sage Gautama, and his wife Ahalya. One day, while Gautama was away, Indra, king of the gods, came to Ahalya disguised as her husband and asked her to be with him. Here the versions part, and it matters which you're hearing. In Valmiki's telling, Ahalya sees through the disguise. She knows it's Indra, and she agrees, the text says, out of curiosity about the king of the gods. Some later tellings say she was fully deceived, and never knew. Either way, Gautama comes home, sees Indra slipping out, still wearing the sage's own form, and in his fury curses them both. Indra is cursed and humiliated. And to Ahalya, Gautama says: you will stay here, for thousands of years, unseen by any living being, living on air, lying in ash, doing penance. And then he adds the part that's easy to miss. When Rama comes to this forest and you welcome him as a guest, you'll be free of this, and you'll return to me in your own form. Then Gautama leaves for the Himalaya. So the empty hermitage isn't empty at all. Someone has been there the whole time, through years and years, unseen, waiting for a guest. Vishvamitra turns to Rama and says: go in. Help her. Tomorrow, what happens when he does.
screen: `GAUTAMA'S HERMITAGE, EMPTY.` · `INDRA IN DISGUISE.` · `THE VERSIONS PART.` · `THE CURSE, AND ITS END.` · then, large: `UNSEEN, WAITING FOR A GUEST.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of someone in your life who might feel unseen: someone who's been quietly carrying something, or who's been left out, or who made a mistake and has been paying for it a long time. Don't judge their story. Just picture them, and on each breath out, let a little warmth go their way, the way you'd look up and really see someone. The bell holds the time.
Ahalya restored. Gautama's wife, cursed to live unseen in an empty hermitage until Rama comes and she welcomes him as a guest.

Your line: Ahalya restored. Today, look for one person who's usually overlooked, at work, in your family, in a shop, and really see them: their name, their eyes, a real thank you. Day five hundred five.

that it ends when she welcomes Rama as a guest.

what it means: the tellings differ on what she knew; in all of them, her curse carries its own end.

506.title: Ahalya restored
506.hook: she isn't stone, and she isn't only rescued: in Valmiki, she is the host
506.howItsDone: In much of popular Hindu tradition, Ahalya is freed from stone by the touch of Rama's foot, a scene loved for what it says about Rama's grace; Valmiki's version, where she is invisible and freed by hosting him, is often taught alongside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ahalya restored, part one. An empty hermitage, a curse, and someone unseen there for years, waiting for a guest. Did you really see someone who's usually overlooked? Day five hundred six.

On television, in comic books, from a grandmother's lap, the scene usually goes like this. A stone lies by the path. Rama's foot brushes it. And the stone becomes a woman. It's a beautiful picture, and an old one. But it isn't Valmiki's. In Valmiki's Sanskrit, there's no stone at all, and no foot brushing against one. What happens instead is quieter, and in some ways more striking, and it starts with a woman nobody can see.
screen: `A STONE BY THE PATH.` → `RAMA'S FOOT TOUCHES IT.` → `NOT IN VALMIKI.`

segments.voice: Rama walks into the hermitage, with Vishvamitra and Lakshmana behind him. And there she is. Ahalya, shining with the power of her long penance, the text says, but hidden, like a flame wrapped in smoke, like the moon behind a cloud, like sunlight dazzling on water, so bright you can't quite look at it. Until now, no one could see her at all. Now Rama sees her, and the curse is over. And then the brothers do something remarkable. Rama and Lakshmana take hold of Ahalya's feet, the gesture of respect you'd show an elder. These two princes bow to a woman the world has been looking away from for years. Ahalya remembers Gautama's words, and she does exactly what the curse said would free her: she receives them as guests. She brings water to wash their feet, offers them welcome, honors them as a host honors guests. Flowers fall from the sky. Drums sound in heaven. And Gautama, returning, is reunited with her, and together they honor Rama. Look at the shape of it. She isn't lifted out of a rock by a foot. She's seen, she's honored, and she acts. The one being rescued is also the one offering hospitality. In the tellings where she becomes stone, the scene says something about Rama's grace. In Valmiki, it also says something about her: after all those years, she's still a host.
screen: `A FLAME WRAPPED IN SMOKE.` · `THE PRINCES TOUCH HER FEET.` · `SHE RECEIVES THEM AS GUESTS.` · `GAUTAMA RETURNS.` · then, large: `SEEN, HONORED, AND HOSTING.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Picture yourself as host for a moment. Someone you care about is arriving. Imagine opening the door, offering a glass of water, saying welcome. Feel what it's like to give, even on a day when you yourself feel tired or overlooked. Breathe with that small act of welcome. Let it be enough. The bell holds the time.
Ahalya restored. Seen at last by Rama, honored by the princes, and freed as she welcomes them as guests, then reunited with Gautama.
Your line: Ahalya restored. Today, be a host to someone, even in a tiny way: a glass of water, a chair pulled out, a real welcome. Day five hundred six.

507.title: Janaka's bow
507.hook: a priest asks about his mother, and a king tells where his bow, and his daughter, came from
507.howItsDone: Hindus celebrate Sita's appearance from the earth on Sita Navami, in the month of Vaishakha, and Mithila, in today's Bihar and Nepal's Janakpur region, holds her as its own daughter.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ahalya restored, part two. Not stone in Valmiki, but unseen, and freed by being seen and hosting her guests. Did you welcome someone? Today, Mithila. Day five hundred seven.

The travelers reach Mithila, and King Janaka comes out to receive them with his priests. One of them is Shatananda, Janaka's chief priest. And the first thing he asks Vishvamitra isn't about the bow, or the princes, or the sacrifice. He asks: did you show my mother to Rama? Was she honored? Did my father come back to her? Shatananda is Ahalya and Gautama's eldest son. Yesterday's story was his family's. And when he hears yes, she's free, they're together, he's overjoyed. Then the king speaks of something else.
screen: `MITHILA, AND ITS PRIEST.` → `DID YOU SHOW MY MOTHER TO RAMA?` → `YES. SHE'S FREE.`

segments.voice: Vishvamitra says: these boys would like to see the bow. And Janaka tells its story. Long ago, at the great sacrifice of Daksha, Shiva was refused his share of the offerings. In anger he raised this very bow against the gods, ready to cut them down. The gods begged him to relent, and he did, and he gave them the bow. The gods gave it to Devarata, an ancestor of Janaka's line, as something to keep. It has stayed in Mithila ever since. A bow that once threatened the gods. Then Janaka tells a second story, about his daughter. Once, he says, I was plowing a field to prepare for a sacrifice, and out of the earth, from the furrow the plow had cut, a girl rose up. I raised her as my own, and named her Sita. Sita means furrow, the line a plow cuts. She wasn't born from a womb, the text says. She came from the earth itself. That's why she's often called Bhumija, daughter of the earth, and Janaki, daughter of Janaka. So in one speech, the king puts two things side by side: a bow of Shiva, kept for generations, and a daughter of the soil, raised with love. And he's decided that only the one who can handle the first can marry the second. Tomorrow, what that has cost him.
screen: `SHATANANDA, AHALYA'S SON.` · `SHIVA'S BOW, RAISED AT DAKSHA'S RITE.` · `KEPT BY JANAKA'S LINE.` · `SITA RISES FROM THE FURROW.` · then, large: `SĪTĀ: THE FURROW.`

segments.voice: Sit and feel the ground beneath you. The floor, then the building's foundation, then the earth under that. Let your weight sink into it. Imagine, for a moment, that you came from this ground the way Sita did: held by it, fed by it. Breathe in, and feel the earth support you. Breathe out, and give your weight back to it. The bell holds the time.
Janaka's bow. The bow of Shiva, kept in Mithila since Daksha's sacrifice, and the test Janaka sets for whoever would marry Sita, the daughter of the furrow.
Your line: Janaka's bow. Today, spend one minute outdoors with your feet on real ground, grass or soil, and remember where food, and Sita, come from. Day five hundred seven.

508.title: Janaka's bow
508.hook: kings who couldn't lift it decided to take Mithila instead
508.howItsDone: Across India, the contest of the bow is staged in Ramlila performances; later retellings such as the Ramcharitmanas present it as a swayamvara, while Valmiki describes Sita as viryashulka, won by strength.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Janaka's bow, part one. Shiva's bow from Daksha's sacrifice, and Sita rising from the furrow. Did you stand on real ground for a minute? Day five hundred eight.

Janaka made a decision about his daughter, and he announced it. Sita, he said, is viryashulka. The price of her hand is strength. Not gold, not alliances, not land. Whoever can lift and string Shiva's bow may marry her. Word spread. Kings came from everywhere to try. And every one of them failed. And then, Janaka tells Vishvamitra, something ugly happened. Wounded pride doesn't always go home quietly. Sometimes it comes back with an army.
screen: `THE PRICE OF HER HAND: STRENGTH.` → `KINGS COME FROM EVERYWHERE.` → `EVERY ONE OF THEM FAILS.`

segments.voice: Janaka tells it plainly. The kings who failed were furious. They felt insulted, mocked by a bow. So they joined forces and laid siege to Mithila. For a whole year, the city was surrounded. Supplies ran low. Janaka, who couldn't match their armies, turned to austerity and prayer, and the gods answered him with an army of their own. The kings were scattered and fled. So when Janaka shows Rama the bow, he's not showing off a party trick. He's showing a test that has already cost his city a war, and he knows what happens when proud men fail it. And Janaka says: if Rama can string this bow, I'll give him Sita. Then he orders it brought out. Valmiki makes the scene huge. The bow lies in an iron chest, on a cart with eight wheels, and the text says it takes five thousand tall, strong men to haul it in, with great effort. They set it down before the king and the guests. Think about what Rama is looking at. Not just weight. A bow a god once aimed at the gods. A line of kings who failed and turned to violence. A father who will give his daughter only for real strength. And the whole hall, waiting to see what the young prince will do.
screen: `VIRYASHULKA: STRENGTH AS BRIDE-PRICE.` · `THE KINGS FAIL, AND BESIEGE MITHILA.` · `THE GODS ANSWER JANAKA.` · `AN EIGHT-WHEELED CART, FIVE THOUSAND MEN.` · then, large: `THE HALL WAITS.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of a time something didn't go your way in front of others, and felt that sting of pride. Let yourself remember it without flinching. Notice the urge, back then or even now, to blame the test, or the person who set it. Breathe that urge out. Breathe in a little more ease. Let the memory sit there, smaller now. The bell holds the time.
Janaka's bow. The bow no king could lift, set as the price of Sita's hand, whose failure led proud kings to besiege Mithila for a year.
Your line: Janaka's bow. Today, if something doesn't go your way, notice the urge to blame the test, and let it pass without acting on it. Day five hundred eight.

509.title: Janaka's bow
509.hook: a bow no king could lift, picked up as if it were nothing, and the sound that follows
509.howItsDone: The breaking of the bow is a high point of Ramlila performances and Ramayana recitations; in many places audiences cheer as the bow snaps, and the scene is often painted and sung at weddings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Janaka's bow, part two. Strength as the bride-price, a city besieged by kings who failed, and a cart hauled by thousands. Did you let an urge to blame the test pass? Day five hundred nine.

The chest is open. The bow lies there, enormous. Nobody in the hall speaks. Vishvamitra looks at Rama and says one short line: Rama, my son, look at the bow. That's all. No speech. Rama steps forward and asks, politely: may I touch it? May I try to lift it, and string it? The king and the sage both say yes. And then, in front of thousands of people, something happens that Valmiki tells in only a few verses.
screen: `THE CHEST IS OPEN.` → `RAMA, MY SON, LOOK AT THE BOW.` → `MAY I TOUCH IT?`

segments.voice: Rama takes hold of the bow in the middle and lifts it, the text says, as if in play. The bow that thousands of men just dragged in on a cart, and that a line of kings couldn't budge. He bends it and strings it. And then he draws the string back, all the way to his ear. And with a crack like thunder, the bow breaks in two. The sound is enormous. The earth shakes like a mountain splitting. Everyone in the hall falls to the ground, stunned, everyone except four: Vishvamitra, King Janaka, Rama and Lakshmana. Notice a few things. Rama asks permission before touching it. He doesn't grab at it the way the angry kings would have. He lifts it lightly, which tells you the strength isn't a strain for him. And he doesn't set out to break it; he draws it fully, the way a bow is meant to be drawn, and it can't hold him. Notice too who stays standing. The teacher, the father, the one who drew it, and the brother who never leaves his side. When the people come to, Janaka speaks, and his words are full of joy. I've seen Rama's strength with my own eyes. Sita will bring glory to our family by marrying him. My promise is fulfilled. And he asks Vishvamitra's leave to send fast messengers to Ayodhya, to bring Dasharatha. The bow is broken. The wedding is coming.
screen: `MAY I TOUCH IT? HE ASKS FIRST.` · `LIFTED AS IF IN PLAY.` · `DRAWN TO THE EAR, IT BREAKS.` · `FOUR STILL STANDING.` · then, large: `THE BOW BREAKS IN TWO.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Imagine picking up something heavy you've been carrying for a long time, a worry, a task, a grudge, and finding it lighter than you thought, as if in play. Breathe in, and lift it. Breathe out, and set it down. Don't force anything. Just let the breath show you how light it could be. The bell holds the time.
Janaka's bow. Rama asks to touch it, lifts it as if in play, strings it, and draws it until it breaks with a crack like thunder.
Your line: Janaka's bow. Today, before you pick up something that isn't yours, a tool, a phone, a task, ask first, the way Rama did. Day five hundred nine.

510.title: the four weddings
510.hook: one wedding becomes four, and two families tell their whole histories first
510.howItsDone: Hindu wedding rites include naming the gotra and ancestors of the bride's and groom's families, a custom echoed in Vasishtha's and Janaka's recitations in the Ramayana.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Janaka's bow, part three. Rama asked first, lifted it as if in play, and the bow broke like thunder. Did you ask before picking up something that wasn't yours? Day five hundred ten.

Janaka's messengers ride hard to Ayodhya. They stand before Dasharatha, the king who not long ago begged a sage not to take his young son, and they tell him: your Rama broke Shiva's bow. Your Lakshmana is with him, safe. King Janaka asks you to come to Mithila for the wedding. You can imagine the old man's face. The next morning, Dasharatha sets out with Vasishtha, his priests, his army and his treasure, and travels to Mithila. When the two kings meet, Janaka welcomes him like family before they are family.
screen: `MESSENGERS RIDE TO AYODHYA.` → `YOUR RAMA BROKE SHIVA'S BOW.` → `TWO KINGS EMBRACE.`

segments.voice: Before anyone marries, the families do something we might find surprising. They recite their family trees, aloud, all the way back. Vasishtha stands and names the line of Ikshvaku, generation after generation: from Brahma, through Manu, Ikshvaku himself, kings like Sagara, whose sons dug deep into the earth, and Bhagiratha, who brought the Ganga down from heaven, all the way to Dasharatha. Then Janaka names his own line from King Nimi down, including Devarata, who received the bow. Why? Because in this world a wedding isn't two people meeting. It's two long stories joining. Then Janaka makes the formal gift. Sita to Rama. And his second daughter, Urmila, to Lakshmana. And then a lovely thing happens. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha together suggest something more. Janaka's younger brother, Kushadhvaja, has two daughters too, Mandavi and Shrutakirti. Why not give them to Bharata and Shatrughna? Janaka agrees with joy. So one wedding becomes four. Four brothers, four sisters and cousins, two royal houses woven together in a single day. Before the ceremony, Dasharatha gives away an enormous gift of cows in his sons' names, and a final guest arrives: Yudhajit, Bharata's uncle from Kaikeyi's family. From now on, whatever happens in Ayodhya happens to Mithila too.
screen: `THE FAMILY TREES, ALOUD.` · `SITA TO RAMA, URMILA TO LAKSHMANA.` · `MANDAVI AND SHRUTAKIRTI, TOO.` · `ONE WEDDING BECOMES FOUR.` · then, large: `TWO HOUSES, ONE DAY.`

Just feel the line of them, stretching back, ending here, in this breath. If you pray, you can remember them in your own way. Breathe in, and feel them behind you. The bell holds the time.
The four weddings. Rama and Sita, Lakshmana and Urmila, Bharata and Mandavi, Shatrughna and Shrutakirti: two royal houses joined in one day.

511.title: the four weddings
511.hook: a father puts his daughter's hand in a young man's hand and says one sentence
511.howItsDone: In Hindu weddings, the kanyadana, the father's giving of the bride's hand, and the circling of the sacred fire are central rites; some families recall Janaka's words to Rama when they explain them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the four weddings, part one. Two family trees recited aloud, and one wedding becoming four. Did you ask someone about the people who came before them? Today, the ceremony, and a week closes. Day five hundred eleven.

If you've been to a Hindu wedding, you may know the moment, though customs vary from family to family. The fire is lit in the middle of the canopy. The priest is chanting. And the bride's father stands, takes his daughter's hand, and places it in the groom's hand. Rooms full of noisy relatives go quiet for it. That moment has an echo in the Ramayana. Janaka, the king who found his daughter in a furrow, brings Sita to the altar, decked in jewels, and stands her across from Rama, by the fire.

segments.voice: Janaka speaks to Rama, and his words begin: iyam sita mama suta sahadharmachari tava. This is Sita, my daughter, your companion in dharma. Accept her. Take her hand in yours. She will be devoted to you, and will follow you always, like your shadow. Then he pours sacred water, and the gods say well done. Sahadharmachari is the key word. Saha, together. Dharma, the right way, duty, the path. Chari, one who walks. One who walks the path of dharma together with you. Not a possession, not a prize, though she was won by strength: a companion on the way. Janaka gives Urmila to Lakshmana, and his brother's daughters to Bharata and Shatrughna, with similar words. Then the four couples circle the fire, keeping it on their right, three times. Flowers fall from the sky, heavenly drums sound, and the apsaras dance. The next morning Vishvamitra says goodbye and leaves for the northern mountains. The sage who took two boys from their father's house leaves them married, with their father and brothers around them. Now the week, from the top. An empty hermitage, and Indra's disguise. Ahalya seen, honored, and hosting. Shatananda's question, and Sita rising from the furrow. The siege of the failed kings. The bow breaking like thunder. Two family trees recited. And today, four couples circling one fire, and a father's sentence about walking together.

original.note: Sanskrit sahadharmacarī: she who walks the path of dharma together with you. saha (together) + dharma + carī (one who walks).
